910.name: Prehistoric Iberia
910.description: The Iberian Peninsula boasts some of Europe's most spectacular prehistoric heritage, from the Altamira cave paintings to Megalithic cultures. Iberians, Celts, and Celtiberians formed the rich pre-Roman ethnic tapestry.

sub_clusters.name: Altamira & Paleolithic Art
sub_clusters.description: The Altamira cave paintings (c. 15,000 BCE), El Castillo and other Cantabrian cave art sites, and the Ice Age cultures of the Iberian Peninsula.
key_events: Altamira cave paintings created – masterwork of Paleolithic art (c. 15,000 BCE)

sub_clusters.name: Iberians, Celts & Tartessos
sub_clusters.description: The Iberian tribes, the Celtic and Celtiberian peoples, the mysterious Tartessos civilisation in the south, and Phoenician and Greek colonial contacts along the Mediterranean coast.

910.name: Roman Hispania
910.description: Rome's conquest of Hispania during the Punic Wars created one of the empire's most important provinces. Hispania produced emperors (Trajan, Hadrian, Theodosius), the philosopher Seneca, and a thoroughly Romanised civilisation.

sub_clusters.name: Punic Wars & Roman Conquest
sub_clusters.description: Scipio Africanus's campaigns against Carthage in Iberia, the siege of Numantia (133 BCE), the Sertorian War, and Augustus's final conquest of Cantabria and Asturias.
key_events: Scipio defeats Carthaginians at Ilipa; Rome gains Hispania (206 BCE)
Siege and fall of Numantia – symbol of Celtiberian resistance (133 BCE)

sub_clusters.name: Imperial Hispania & Romanisation
sub_clusters.description: The golden age of Roman Hispania: Trajan, Hadrian, and Theodosius as emperors of Hispanic origin, the cities of Tarraco, Emerita Augusta, and Hispalis, the spread of Christianity, and the Visigothic invasions.

920.name: Visigoths & Al-Andalus
920.description: The Visigothic Kingdom of Toledo unified Hispania until the devastating Umayyad conquest of 711. Al-Andalus became one of medieval Europe's most brilliant civilisations, with Córdoba as the intellectual capital of the Western world.

sub_clusters.name: Visigothic Kingdom of Toledo
sub_clusters.description: The Germanic Visigoths' kingdom centred on Toledo, Reccared's conversion to Catholicism (589), the Councils of Toledo, the Visigothic legal code (Liber Iudiciorum), and the kingdom's collapse before the Umayyad invasion.
key_events: Umayyad forces under Tariq ibn Ziyad defeat the Visigoths at Guadalete (711)

sub_clusters.name: Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba
sub_clusters.description: Abd al-Rahman I's establishment of the Emirate of Córdoba (756), its elevation to a caliphate (929), Córdoba as Europe's largest and most cultured city, the Great Mosque, and the Taifa fragmentation after 1031.
key_events: Abd al-Rahman III declares the Caliphate of Córdoba (929)

920.name: The Reconquista
920.description: The Reconquista was the centuries-long Christian reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule. Beginning at Covadonga (718), it produced the kingdoms of Asturias, León, Castile, Navarre, and Aragon, and culminated in the fall of Granada (1492).

sub_clusters.name: Covadonga & Northern Christian Kingdoms
sub_clusters.description: Pelayo's legendary stand at Covadonga, the kingdom of Asturias, the repopulation of the Duero valley, the rise of León and Castile, and the capture of Toledo by Alfonso VI (1085).
key_events: Alfonso VI of Castile captures Toledo (1085)

sub_clusters.name: El Cid & the High Reconquista
sub_clusters.description: El Cid's legend, the Almoravid and Almohad invasions from North Africa, the decisive Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa (1212), and Ferdinand III's conquest of Córdoba (1236) and Seville (1248).
key_events: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa – turning point of the Reconquista (1212)

sub_clusters.name: Fall of Granada (1492)
sub_clusters.description: The Nasrid Kingdom of Granada as the last Muslim state, the marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella uniting Castile and Aragon, the final siege and fall of Granada (2 January 1492), and the expulsion of Jews.
key_events: Fall of Granada – end of the Reconquista (2 Jan 1492)
Alhambra Decree expels Jews from Spain (31 March 1492)

930.name: Catholic Monarchs & Columbus
930.description: Ferdinand and Isabella's marriage united Spain's two great kingdoms. Their patronage of Columbus's 1492 voyage, the conquest of Granada, the establishment of the Inquisition, and the unification of Spain transformed a peninsular kingdom into a global power.

sub_clusters.name: Unification & the Spanish Inquisition
sub_clusters.description: The marriage of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile (1469), the establishment of the Spanish Inquisition (1478) under Torquemada, and the creation of a unified Spanish state.
key_events: Spanish Inquisition established under Torquemada (1478)

sub_clusters.name: Columbus & the New World
sub_clusters.description: Columbus's first voyage (1492), the Treaty of Tordesillas with Portugal (1494), the beginning of the Spanish colonial empire in the Americas, and the succession to Charles I (Charles V of the HRE).
key_events: Columbus reaches the Americas (12 Oct 1492)
Treaty of Tordesillas divides the New World (1494)

930.name: Habsburg Spain & the Global Empire
930.description: Under Charles V and Philip II, Spain became the world's first truly global empire—'the empire on which the sun never sets.' But the costs of constant warfare, the Dutch Revolt, the Armada's defeat, and economic mismanagement led to a long decline.

sub_clusters.name: Charles V & the Universal Monarchy
sub_clusters.description: Charles V ruling Spain, the Netherlands, the HRE, and the American empire simultaneously, the conquest of the Aztec and Inca empires, the Council of Trent, and his abdication dividing the realm.
key_events: Hernán Cortés conquers the Aztec Empire (1519–21)

sub_clusters.name: Philip II & the Spanish Armada
sub_clusters.description: Philip II's reign from El Escorial, the Battle of Lepanto (1571), the Dutch Revolt, the disastrous Spanish Armada (1588), and Spain's role as champion of Counter-Reformation Catholicism.
key_events: Battle of Lepanto – Christian fleet defeats Ottoman navy (1571)
Spanish Armada defeated by England (1588)

sub_clusters.name: Siglo de Oro & Habsburg Decline
sub_clusters.description: The cultural Golden Age (Cervantes, Velázquez, Calderón) amidst military and economic decline, the Thirty Years' War, the loss of Portugal (1640) and the Netherlands, and the extinction of the Spanish Habsburg line.
key_events: Cervantes publishes Don Quixote (1605)

940.name: Bourbon Spain & Enlightenment
940.description: The War of the Spanish Succession installed the Bourbon dynasty. The 18th century brought centralisation (Nueva Planta decrees), Enlightenment reforms under Charles III, and alliance with France, before Napoleon's betrayal shattered the old order.

sub_clusters.name: War of the Spanish Succession
sub_clusters.description: The succession crisis after Charles II's death, the devastating War of the Spanish Succession, the Nueva Planta decrees abolishing Aragonese and Catalan autonomy, and the Treaty of Utrecht.
key_events: Treaty of Utrecht – Philip V confirmed as King; Spain loses European territories (1713)

sub_clusters.name: Charles III & Enlightenment Reforms
sub_clusters.description: The Bourbon reforms, Charles III's modernisation of Madrid and the colonial administration, the expulsion of the Jesuits (1767), and the economic revival of the 18th century.

940.name: Peninsular War & Loss of Empire
940.description: Napoleon's invasion provoked a national uprising and the Peninsular War. The liberal Constitution of Cádiz (1812) was a milestone in constitutional history. Spain lost virtually its entire American empire by 1825 and its last colonies in the Spanish-American War of 1898.

sub_clusters.name: Peninsular War & Cádiz Constitution
sub_clusters.description: Napoleon's deposition of the Spanish Bourbons, the popular uprising of Dos de Mayo (1808), guerrilla warfare, Wellington's campaigns, and the liberal Cortes of Cádiz producing the 1812 Constitution.
key_events: Dos de Mayo uprising in Madrid against Napoleon (2 May 1808)
Cortes of Cádiz promulgate liberal constitution (19 March 1812)

sub_clusters.name: Carlist Wars & Political Instability
sub_clusters.description: Fernando VII's absolutist restoration, the three Carlist Wars pitting liberals against traditionalists, the brief First Republic (1873), and chronic political instability.

sub_clusters.name: Spanish-American War & 'El Desastre' (1898)
sub_clusters.description: The Restoration monarchy under Alfonso XII and the regency, the loss of Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines, and Guam in the Spanish-American War of 1898—the 'Disaster' that provoked the Generation of '98 intellectual movement.
key_events: Treaty of Paris – Spain cedes Cuba, Puerto Rico, Philippines (10 Dec 1898)

950.name: Second Republic & Spanish Civil War
950.description: Spain's tumultuous early 20th century saw Primo de Rivera's dictatorship, the hopeful Second Republic, and the devastating Civil War (1936–39)—a prelude to World War II that attracted international volunteers and became a symbol of the struggle between democracy and fascism.

sub_clusters.name: Primo de Rivera & Second Republic
sub_clusters.description: The Rif War, Primo de Rivera's dictatorship (1923–30), Alfonso XIII's exile, the euphoric proclamation of the Second Republic (1931), radical reforms, and the polarisation leading to military revolt.
key_events: Second Spanish Republic proclaimed (14 April 1931)

sub_clusters.name: Spanish Civil War (1936–1939)
sub_clusters.description: Franco's Nationalist uprising, the Siege of the Alcázar, the bombing of Guernica by the Condor Legion (1937, immortalised by Picasso), the International Brigades, the fall of Barcelona and Madrid, and the Nationalist victory.
key_events: Bombing of Guernica by the German Condor Legion (26 April 1937)
Spanish Civil War ends with Franco's victory (1 April 1939)

950.name: Franco Dictatorship
950.description: Francisco Franco's 36-year authoritarian rule isolated Spain from democratic Europe. The regime evolved from fascist autarky to technocratic developmentalism, while brutally suppressing regional identities, political opposition, and civil liberties.

sub_clusters.name: Francoism – Autarky & International Isolation
sub_clusters.description: Post-war repression, the White Terror, international isolation, WWII neutrality (with pro-Axis Blue Division), the US bases agreement (1953) breaking the isolation, and economic stagnation.
key_events: Spain signs military bases agreement with the United States (1953)

sub_clusters.name: Technocratic Developmentalism & Social Change
sub_clusters.description: The 1959 Stabilisation Plan, the 'Spanish Miracle' of economic growth, mass tourism, labour migration, the emergence of clandestine opposition (CCOO, ETA), and Franco's death on 20 November 1975.
key_events: ETA assassinates PM Carrero Blanco (20 Dec 1973)
Francisco Franco dies (20 Nov 1975)

960.name: Democratic Transition (La Transición)
960.description: Spain's peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy under King Juan Carlos I and PM Adolfo Suárez was one of the 20th century's most remarkable political transformations. The 1978 Constitution, the defeat of the 23-F coup attempt, and EEC accession defined the era.

sub_clusters.name: Suárez & the 1978 Constitution
sub_clusters.description: King Juan Carlos's appointment of Adolfo Suárez, the legalisation of political parties (including the Communist Party), the landmark 1978 Constitution establishing a parliamentary monarchy with autonomous communities.
key_events: Spanish Constitution approved by referendum (6 Dec 1978)

sub_clusters.name: 23-F Coup Attempt & Democratic Consolidation
sub_clusters.description: Lt Col Tejero's seizure of the Cortes (23 February 1981), King Juan Carlos's televised defence of democracy, Felipe González's socialist government (1982), and Spain's accession to the EEC and NATO.
key_events: 23-F coup attempt – Tejero storms the Cortes (23 Feb 1981)
Spain joins the EEC (1 Jan 1986)

960.name: Modern Spain & European Integration
960.description: Spain's integration into Europe brought spectacular modernisation. The annus mirabilis of 1992 (Barcelona Olympics, Seville Expo, Madrid Cultural Capital) showcased a confident, democratic Spain, while ETA terrorism remained a persistent threat.

sub_clusters.name: 1992 – Annus Mirabilis
sub_clusters.description: The González era, EU structural funds transforming infrastructure, the Barcelona Olympics (1992), Seville Expo, the AVE high-speed rail, and Spain's emergence as a modern European state.
key_events: Barcelona Olympic Games showcase democratic Spain (1992)

sub_clusters.name: Aznar Era & Madrid Train Bombings
sub_clusters.description: José María Aznar's centre-right government, Spain's economic boom, the Prestige oil disaster (2002), the Iraq War controversy, and the devastating 11-M Madrid train bombings (2004) killing 193 people.
key_events: 11-M Madrid train bombings kill 193 (11 March 2004)

960.name: Contemporary Spain
960.description: 21st-century Spain has navigated the 2008 financial crisis, record unemployment, the end of ETA, and the dramatic Catalan independence crisis, while its democracy has matured through coalition politics and social reforms.

sub_clusters.name: Financial Crisis & Austerity
sub_clusters.description: Zapatero's social reforms, the bursting of the housing bubble (2008), the sovereign debt crisis, 27% unemployment, EU bailout of Spanish banks (2012), the Indignados/15-M movement, and the rise of Podemos and Ciudadanos.

sub_clusters.name: Catalan Crisis & New Politics
sub_clusters.description: The illegal 2017 Catalan independence referendum, the declaration of independence and Article 155 suspension of autonomy, the imprisonment and later pardoning of separatist leaders, and the ETA dissolution (2018).
key_events: Catalan independence referendum and declaration (1 Oct & 27 Oct 2017)
ETA announces permanent dissolution (May 2018)

sub_clusters.name: Post-Pandemic Spain
sub_clusters.description: Spain's severe COVID-19 impact, the EU recovery fund, coalition government under Sánchez, the Democratic Memory Law confronting the Franco era, and ongoing territorial and political debates.

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
